disposition_reason: Both ancient accounts describe the decisive defeat of the revolt but neither names the place, so it is drawn as a halo over the Watling Street corridor in the Midlands, not a pin.
title: The final defeat of Boudica's revolt
candidate_description: Suetonius Paulinus, with a much smaller force, chose a defile backed by woodland and defeated the rebel army; Boudica died soon after (by poison in Tacitus, by illness in Dio).
place: Probably along Watling Street, English Midlands (site unknown)
uncertainty_note: Neither Tacitus nor Dio names the site. It is usually placed on or near Watling Street between London and Wroxeter; candidates include Mancetter (Manduessedum) and High Cross on the Warwickshire/Leicestershire border and Church Stowe in Northamptonshire, and some writers argue for sites well outside this halo. No battlefield archaeology has been confirmed. Tacitus's figures (80,000 Britons, 400 Romans killed) are not taken as reliable. The revolt is dated AD 60 or 61: Tacitus places it (with the attack on Mona) under the consuls of 61, but many scholars read his annalistic grouping as covering 60–61 and put the outbreak in 60; the atlas uses 60 (circa) for every revolt row.
facets: Evidence type=ancient narratives|Dating basis=historical narrative|Interpretation=on or near Watling Street; Mancetter often proposed

title: All Saints' church, Brixworth
candidate_description: One of the largest surviving Anglo-Saxon churches in England: an aisled basilica with arcades and arches turned in reused Roman brick and tile, later given a western tower, stair turret and polygonal apse.
uncertainty_note: The building is certain; its date is not. A 12th-century Peterborough writer, Hugh Candidus, credits the foundation of a monastery at Brixworth to Cuthbald, abbot from about 675, which gave the traditional 7th-century date. disposition_reason: A short entry in a chronicle written in Gaul in 452 says that the British provinces had passed under Saxon control; drawn as a halo over Britain because it names no place, and how much of Britain it means is debated.
title: The Gallic Chronicle: 'the Britains' pass to the Saxons
candidate_description: The anonymous Gallic Chronicle of 452 records, under a year equal to about 440–441, that the Britains, after long troubles and various disasters, were brought under the power of the Saxons. The later Chronicle of 511 has a parallel entry under 440.
place: Britain (the British provinces; no place named)
uncertainty_note: The entry certainly exists, but its date and meaning are debated. Mommsen's 1892 edition placed it at 441–2; Muhlberger argued the best manuscripts give the year before, and modern editions usually date it 440–441, so the window is 440–441. Molly Miller argued the date was an editorial artefact and the chronicle later reworked; Jones and Casey used it to date the Saxon takeover. The chronicler wrote in southern Gaul and probably knew most about the parts of Britain facing the Continent, so few historians read it as the fall of the whole island; the halo reflects the province named, not a region of Saxon control.

disposition_reason: Patrick's own Confessio and Letter to Coroticus describe his captivity in Ireland and his return there as a bishop; drawn as a halo over the north and west of Ireland because his writings name only the wood of Foclut 'near the western sea'.
title: Patrick's mission in Ireland
candidate_description: Patrick, a Romano-British Christian taken to Ireland as a slave at about sixteen, escaped after six years and later returned as a bishop, baptising and ordaining clergy among the Irish, as he describes in his Confessio and his Letter to the soldiers of Coroticus.
place: Northern and western Ireland (the wood of Foclut 'near the western sea')
uncertainty_note: That Patrick lived and worked in Ireland is certain from his own writings, but they give no dates and name no Irish place except the wood of Foclut near the western sea, which Tírechán in the 7th century placed near Killala, Co. The traditional dates (arrival 432, death 461 or 493) come from annals compiled centuries later that appear to conflate him with Palladius (sent in 431); scholars place him somewhere in the fifth century, several favouring the second half, so the window is wide. The halo covers the north and west, where the earliest tradition places him; it is not his mapped area of work. Later traditions linking him with Armagh, Slemish, Downpatrick and Saul are recorded separately as legend.

disposition_reason: Gildas, born in the year of the battle, records a British victory at the siege of Mount Badon; drawn as a large halo over southern Britain because the place has never been identified and the date is known only within a few decades.
title: Siege of Mount Badon (Mons Badonicus)

uncertainty_note: The only near-contemporary source is one ambiguous sentence of Gildas (De excidio 26): Badon was in the year of his birth, 44 years (and a month) before he wrote, or 44 years after an earlier point. The halo covers the main southern proposals, not a known battlefield.

title: The Great Army takes York
candidate_description: The 'great heathen army', which had landed in East Anglia in 865, crossed the Humber and seized York in late 866. The rival Northumbrian kings Osberht and Ælla joined forces and broke into the city on 21 March 867, but both were killed and the Vikings held York.
uncertainty_note: The Chronicle (s.a. 867, its year beginning in the autumn) and Asser give only the year, which places the capture in late 866. The day, 1 November (All Saints), comes from later northern sources, chiefly the Historia regum attributed to Symeon of Durham, as reported by Smyth; some modern accounts give 21 November instead, so the month is shown, not the day. The date of the failed Northumbrian counter-attack, 21 March 867, rests on the same northern tradition. The pin marks the city; where in it the fighting took place is not recorded.

disposition_reason: One version of the Chronicle records that the northern and western kings made peace with Æthelstan 'at Eamont' on 12 July; drawn as a halo because the meeting place is known only as the river near Penrith, with a later writer placing part of it at Dacre.
title: Kings submit to Æthelstan at Eamont
candidate_description: After taking York in 927 on the death of Sihtric, Æthelstan met Hywel, king of the West Welsh, Constantine, king of the Scots, Owain, king of the people of Gwent, and Ealdred son of Eadwulf of Bamburgh at Eamont on 12 July. They made peace with pledges and oaths and renounced idolatry, accepting Æthelstan's overlordship.
uncertainty_note: The only near-contemporary record, Chronicle MS D, enters the meeting under 926; it is dated 927 because Sihtric's death, which it follows, is placed in 927 by the Irish annals. D says only 'at Eamont' (æt Eamotum), the river that runs east from Ullswater past Eamont Bridge to the Eden. William of Malmesbury (12th century) places at least part of the meeting at Dacre, about 5 km west, where Constantine's son was baptised, and names Owain as king of the Cumbrians (Strathclyde) rather than of Gwent. Which Owain was present, whether 'Hywel of the West Welsh' is Hywel Dda or a Cornish ruler, and the suggested settings at Mayburgh Henge or King Arthur's Round Table, are unresolved. The halo covers Eamont Bridge and Dacre.

disposition_reason: The Chronicle records that the Northumbrians drove out their king Eric in 954 and that Eadred took the kingdom; drawn as a halo over the kingdom of York because no source says where the expulsion happened.
title: Eric expelled from York; Eadred takes Northumbria
candidate_description: In 954 the Northumbrians drove out Eric, the last independent Scandinavian king of York, and the English king Eadred took over Northumbria. A 13th-century chronicle says Eric was then betrayed by Earl Oswulf and killed by Maccus at Stainmore.
uncertainty_note: The Chronicle says only that the Northumbrians drove Eric out; it gives no place. The halo is centred on York, the seat of the kingdom, and covers its heartland, not a point. Eric's death at Stainmore, the Pennine pass on the A66 about 100 km north-west of York, is reported only by Roger of Wendover in the 13th century, perhaps from lost northern annals, so it is described here and not drawn; the local tradition linking the Rey Cross to his grave is unsupported (no burial was found when it was excavated in 1990). Eric of York is usually identified with the Norwegian king Eiríkr blóðøx (Eric Bloodaxe) of the sagas, but Clare Downham (2004) has questioned this.

title: Edgar consecrated king at Bath
candidate_description: On Whitsunday, 11 May 973, Edgar, king since 959, was consecrated king at Bath by Archbishops Dunstan and Oswald in an elaborate ceremony, with his queen Ælfthryth also anointed; soon afterwards he took his fleet to Chester, where several kings of Britain pledged to be his allies.
uncertainty_note: The ceremony took place in the minster church at Bath, but the Anglo-Saxon church has not been found; it probably lay at least partly under the present abbey, and recent excavations found early apsed buildings just to its south. The pin marks the present abbey. The day is Pentecost (Whitsunday) 973, which fell on 11 May. Why Edgar was consecrated so late in his reign is debated. The meeting at Chester is recorded in the Chronicle as six kings pledging to be his allies; the story that eight kings rowed him on the Dee is a later embellishment (recorded separately as excluded).

disposition_reason: The Chronicle records that Ealdorman Byrhtnoth was killed fighting a Viking army at Maldon in 991, and an Old English poem describes the battle; drawn as a halo around the registered battlefield opposite Northey Island, whose identification is widely accepted but not proved.
title: Battle of Maldon
candidate_description: A Viking fleet that had raided Folkestone, Sandwich and Ipswich came to Maldon in Essex, where Ealdorman Byrhtnoth and the Essex levies fought it and were defeated; Byrhtnoth was killed. In the same year, on the advice of Archbishop Sigeric, the English first paid the Danes tribute, 10,000 pounds.
place: Maldon, Essex (by the causeway to Northey Island)
uncertainty_note: The Chronicle places the battle at Maldon; the day comes from monastic calendars recording Byrhtnoth's death, the Ely calendar giving 10 August and Winchester and Ramsey calendars 11 August. The poem's tidal crossing to the Viking position was identified by E. D. Laborde (1925) with the causeway to Northey Island, and the mainland opposite is the registered battlefield; this is widely accepted but has been challenged, and the poet's geography may be stylised. Only MS A names the leader, Olaf (Anlaf), with 93 ships, in an annal entered under 993; whether he was Olaf Tryggvason is an inference. The halo covers the registered battlefield and the town.

disposition_reason: The Chronicle records Æthelred's order to kill the Danish men in England on 13 November 1002, and a royal charter of 1004 describes the killing of Danes at St Frideswide's church in Oxford; the order applied across England, so the pin marks Oxford, where the evidence is strongest.
title: St Brice's Day massacre
candidate_description: On St Brice's Day, 13 November 1002, King Æthelred II ordered all the Danish men in England to be killed, having been told they meant to kill him and his councillors and seize the kingdom. At Oxford, Danes fleeing the order took refuge in St Frideswide's minster, which was burned.
uncertainty_note: The order and its date are secure, but the Chronicle names no place and gives no numbers: the killings were meant to happen wherever Danes were found, and how widely the order was carried out is unknown. The pin marks Oxford, the only place a contemporary source describes. It stands on Christ Church Cathedral, the traditional site of St Frideswide's minster; no structure of the church burned in 1002 has been found, and the minster's exact site has been debated. The mass grave of young men found at St John's College, Oxford, in 2008 may be victims of the massacre, but radiocarbon dates allow the tenth century as well and the link is not proven.

disposition_reason: The Chronicle records that Swein brought his fleet up the Trent to Gainsborough in 1013, took the submission of the north there and later died there in February 1014; drawn as a pin on the town because the camp itself has not been located.
title: Swein Forkbeard at Gainsborough
candidate_description: King Swein of Denmark sailed into the Humber and up the Trent to Gainsborough in summer 1013, where Earl Uhtred and the Northumbrians, the people of Lindsey and the Five Boroughs submitted to him. He then took the submission of the rest of England, Æthelred fled to Normandy, and Swein was accepted as king until his death at Gainsborough on 3 February 1014.
uncertainty_note: The Chronicle says Swein reached Sandwich before August 1013 and went on quickly to Gainsborough, so his arrival there was in late summer; the day is not given. His death is dated to Candlemas, 'the third day before the nones of February', which is 3 February (Candlemas itself is 2 February). The pin marks the town: where Swein camped and died is not known. Local tradition places a camp at Castle Hills, Thonock, and a royal residence where the Old Hall now stands, but neither has been confirmed by excavation.

disposition_reason: The Chronicle records Cnut's victory over Edmund Ironside at Assandun in Essex, which led to Cnut ruling all England; the site is disputed between Ashingdon and Ashdon, about 56 km apart, so it is drawn as a halo covering both.
title: Battle of Assandun
candidate_description: Cnut defeated Edmund Ironside at Assandun in Essex on 18 October 1016, after Ealdorman Eadric fled the field; many English leaders were killed. Edmund and Cnut then divided the kingdom at Alney (Ola's island) near Deerhurst, and when Edmund died on 30 November 1016 Cnut became king of all England.
place: Assandun, Essex (site disputed: Ashingdon or Ashdon)
uncertainty_note: The battle and its outcome are secure. The place is not: the Chronicle names only 'Assandun' in Essex. The long-standing identification is Ashingdon near Rochford in south-east Essex, where the church on the hill is linked to the minster Cnut built in 1020 for the souls of the dead; Ashdon near Saffron Walden in north-west Essex has also been argued for, and the Battlefields Trust is testing further candidates such as Assington (Suffolk) and Essendon (Hertfordshire), which lie outside the halo. The halo is centred between Ashingdon and Ashdon (about 56 km apart) and covers both; it does not mean the battle was fought between them. The day, 18 October, is the accepted date; the Ely calendar also gives it as the death-day of Bishop Eadnoth, killed in the battle.

disposition_reason: English and Norman sources agree that Edward the Confessor died on 5 January 1066 and was buried in his new church at Westminster, and that Harold was made king the next day; drawn as a pin on Westminster Abbey.
title: Death of Edward the Confessor and coronation of Harold
candidate_description: Edward the Confessor's new church at Westminster was consecrated on 28 December 1065, while the king lay ill. He died on 5 January 1066 and was buried there on 6 January, and on the same day Harold Godwinson, earl of Wessex, was crowned king.
uncertainty_note: Edward's death at Westminster, his burial in the abbey church and Harold's accession are secure. That Harold was crowned in the abbey is the usual, well-founded inference: John of Worcester says he was crowned by Archbishop Ealdred of York on the day of the funeral, while Norman sources and the Bayeux Tapestry name Archbishop Stigand. Edward's church lies beneath the present abbey, which was rebuilt from 1245. Whether Edward named Harold as his successor on his deathbed (the English view) or had earlier promised the crown to William of Normandy, with Harold swearing to support him (the Norman view), is a matter of interpretation.

title: Battle of Clontarf
candidate_description: Brian Bóruma (Brian Boru), king of Munster and claimant to the kingship of all Ireland, with an army from Munster and allies, defeats the men of Leinster under Máel Mórda and the Norse of Dublin with allies from Orkney and the Isles; Brian, his son Murchad and grandson Tairdelbach are killed.
place: Clontarf, north of Dublin Bay (field not located)
uncertainty_note: The battle, its year and the deaths of Brian, Murchad and Tairdelbach are secure in the near-contemporary Annals of Ulster and Annals of Inisfallen. The fighting is placed north of the Liffey, from around the Tolka estuary (Ballybough) eastward along the Clontarf shore; one account has it ranging as far as Kilbarrack. The halo covers that stretch and does not mark a known battlefield.

disposition_reason: Twelfth-century Durham writers record a great battle 'at Carrum' on the Tweed in which the king of Scots, with the king of the Strathclyde Britons, defeated the Northumbrians; the field is not located, so it is drawn as a small halo around Carham.
title: Battle of Carham
candidate_description: Máel Coluim (Malcolm) II, king of Scots, with Owain the Bald, king of the Strathclyde Britons, defeats the Northumbrians at Carham on the Tweed; the English leader is named as Earl Uhtred, though this is doubted.
uncertainty_note: There is no contemporary account; the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle does not mention the battle. Both Durham sources (the Historia Regum and Symeon's Libellus de exordio, written early in the 12th century) give 1018, but the Historia Regum names Uhtred son of Waltheof as the Northumbrian leader, while the Chronicle records Uhtred's killing in 1016. Plummer and Stenton therefore moved the battle to 1016; others, including Duncan (1976), keep 1018 and either doubt the Chronicle's date for Uhtred's death or suppose the leader was his brother Eadwulf Cudel. Carham is named, but no battlefield is known; the halo is centred on the village.
